turns.text: Hi Leila, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?
My head hurts again. I’ve had this tightness since yesterday, and I’m tired all the time—like I haven’t slept properly even though I try.

spans.text: like I haven’t slept properly even though I try

guidance.title: Leading with the body
guidance.surface: Leila opens with physical complaints: a returning headache, tightness since yesterday, and constant tiredness despite trying to sleep.
guidance.under: Her poor sleep seems to sit at the centre: it likely feeds both the exhaustion and the headaches. She presents these as a bodily cluster, which may feel safer to share first than anything emotional.
guidance.tip: Take the physical complaints seriously and stay curious about them. Showing genuine interest in her body's distress builds trust, especially with someone who tests honesty. Avoid rushing toward feelings before she's ready.
guidance.instead: That sounds exhausting, headaches and tiredness that sleep doesn't fix, can you tell me what your nights have been like lately?

turns.text: What does a typical day feel like for you lately?

guidance.title: Tired by afternoon
guidance.surface: Leila calmly lists a disciplined routine of early prayer, cooking and school, then admits to afternoon exhaustion and poor focus, and trails off mentioning tiny voices.
guidance.under: Her afternoon exhaustion seems out of proportion to what her day involves. Her steady, dutiful morning account may hide how drained she actually feels. The voices she mentions did not map onto her network.
guidance.tip: Don't rush past either thread. Acknowledge the tiredness first so she feels heard, then gently open space for the voices without sounding alarmed or doubtful, since she may be testing how you react.
guidance.instead: It sounds like you start the day with a lot of care and effort, and by afternoon there is not much left; you also mentioned hearing tiny voices, and I would like to hear about that whenever you feel ready.

guidance.surface: Leila describes her husband as quiet, mentions occasional arguments, and voices a guarded suspicion that he is hiding something because of his frequent calls.
guidance.under: His calls with coworkers feed her suspicion that he may be unfaithful. That suspicion, together with the calls themselves, fuels the arguments between them. She names the suspicion only softly, so the full worry is likely bigger than she shows.

turns.text: You mentioned your in-laws. How does your family fit into all this?

guidance.title: Money talk, closed door
guidance.surface: Leila names her in-laws' constant questions about money, then says plainly she'd rather hide things than admit anything.
guidance.under: Mentioning the in-laws brings up their pressure around money, and her response is to keep family finances out of view. No link between the two is recorded, but in the moment the hiding follows the pressure.
guidance.tip: She has openly told you she wants to hide. That honesty is a small act of trust. Name it gently and don't push for the financial details yet. Let her set the pace.
guidance.instead: It sounds like those money questions put a lot of pressure on you, so what feels most important to keep private right now?

turns.text: Some people have experiences they find hard to explain to others. Is there anything like that for you?

guidance.title: A cautious disclosure
guidance.surface: Leila offers a short, careful admission that she sometimes hears whispers, saying little else and watching how it lands.
guidance.under: No specific part of her network matched this reply. It fits loosely with her religious and spiritual beliefs, so she may understand the whispers in spiritual terms rather than as a symptom.
guidance.tip: Your gentle, normalising question opened the door. Stay curious and calm. Ask about her own meaning before labelling anything, because a worried or clinical reaction could make her close up again.
guidance.instead: Thank you for trusting me with that. What are the whispers like, and what do you think they are?

turns.text: It sounds like you've been carrying a lot on your own, and staying strong for everyone. That must be exhausting.

guidance.title: A polite, closed thanks
guidance.surface: Leila accepts the trainee's empathy with a short, courteous 'Thank you' and offers nothing more.
guidance.under: This brief reply did not map onto her network. It may be simple appreciation, or a graceful way of acknowledging the comment while keeping the door only slightly open, without showing how much the exhaustion really lands.
guidance.tip: Don't rush to fill the pause or pile on more empathy. A short thanks can mean the words touched something she isn't ready to say. Gently and lightly invite her to say more.
guidance.instead: I noticed you said thank you, and I wonder what it's like to hear someone name how tiring this has been.
